newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller clears third graft charge hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller clears third graft charge hurdle.

text.p: The Turkish parliament voted on Wednesday against sending Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller to the Supreme Court for investigation into the sources of her considerable personal wealth.

Deputy Speaker Kamer Genc said deputies voted 270 to 263 not to impeach Ciller on allegations that her wealth was a result of illegal enrichment. It was the third and final corruption charge vote against her this week.
"Hence it is no longer necessary to send former prime minster Tansu Ciller to the Supreme Court," Genc said after announcing the result.
Impeachment of Ciller would have been a serious blow to the government of Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan.
His eight-month-old coalition is expected to emerge strengthened from the corruption tangle but the powerful military is likely to halt any slide from official secularism.

Conservative Ciller on Tuesday comfortably won votes on two corruption charges relating to the sale of state-owned car maker TOFAS and to the electricity company TEDAS during her time as prime minister between 1993 and 1996.
The opposition's best showing on Tuesday was 257 votes, well short of the 276 that had been needed to impeach Ciller.
A censure motion against Erbakan, set for consideration on February 25, is likewise expected to go the government's way.
Ciller, who is also foreign minister, dismissed opposition charges of rifts in her alliance with Erbakan. "This government will continue," she told a meeting of her True Path Party ahead of the vote.
Stocks in Istanbul ended the day 1.13 percent higher on hopes that Ciller would not be impeached in the final vote. The market closed before the result was announced.
Many MPs from Erbakan's Welfare Party who had backed graft accusations against Ciller when they were in opposition last year voted for her this time, in an about-turn to protect coalition unity.
Erbakan's administration has begun to show cracks recently despite successful joint efforts on privatisation.
Several True Path ministers have criticised plans by Erbakan to increase the profile of Islam in public life.
The proposals are mild but they have sparked wide public debate on Turkey's 70-year-old secularist system and rumours of military intervention against the Islamists.

"Let's not politicise secularism and religion," Ciller said in a call for calm. "We are not going to become a world power by spending our time asking ourselves if we are going to become another Algeria," she said.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algerian violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
The Sabah daily said on Tuesday the head of Turkey's armed forces, General Ismail Hakki Karadayi, would warn Erbakan not to ditch secularism when they talk at a security meeting next week.

"The army is not happy," commentator and military expert Mehmet Ali Birand told Reuters. But he said Erbakan would assure the generals that he has no intention of turning NATO member Turkey into an Islamic state.
"(The meeting) will give us a few months breathing space and then we will start over again," Birand said.
Pro-Western Ciller had previously vowed not to go into coalition with the Islamists but she dropped her strong opposition to Erbakan under a wave of corruption charges.
